Brute Force 001 — a guided SOC investigation
  1 / 1
Start●

You have been handed an alert. Work out what happened.

no experience needed

This is the alert your security team woke up to. Read it before you touch anything:

The alertRepeated failed logons from one external address, then a success on the same account - source 203.0.113.45: 15 failed logons against svc_backup on sec-win-01, then one successful logon, then SMB traffic to an internal host four minutes later.

Your job is to decide one thing: is this a real attack that must be escalated, or a false alarm that can be closed? You will answer it the way a real analyst does — not by guessing, but by following the evidence from the very first search to the last and writing down what you find as you go. By the final card you will know who broke in, with what, into which accounts, on which machines, and when.

What this guide is

It starts at zeroNo security knowledge and no Elastic experience needed. The investigation itself is clicking and reading; the only typing is your report, at the end.
The pictures are realEvery screen picture in this guide is a photograph of the running lab, taken by screenshotting the real Kibana. Nothing is drawn from memory.
It never leaves you guessingAfter every click it says the exact number or text you should now be looking at, and a numbered circle points at the control.
It cleans up after itselfOne file starts the lab — setup-lab.cmd on Windows, setup-lab.sh on macOS or Linux — and one removes it completely. Nothing is left behind.

How to move around

This guide is a deck of cards, one step each. Move through it however you like:

  • The Next and Back buttons at the bottom, or the arrow keys on your keyboard.
  • The row of pills under the header jumps you straight to any step.
  • On a phone, swipe left and right.
  • Press ? any time for help, or the printer icon to save the whole thing as a PDF.

The screen pictures are real screenshots of this lab, running Kibana 9.1.0. Every word, button, column name, row count and timestamp in them is what your own screen will show. The numbers in this guide are not predictions — they were read off these exact screens. If your screen and the picture disagree, stop and follow the If it breaks card near the end before you carry on.

The one thing you need first

Docker Desktop, installed and running. That is the only prerequisite. The lab runs inside it and installs nothing else on your computer. If you do not have Docker Desktop yet, ask your instructor — this lab assumes it is already there.

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You will see all of these in the tool and in your report. Read them once now and the rest of the lab becomes much easier.

The attack

Brute forceGuessing a password by trying many of them until one works. No cleverness at all — just volume, and patience.
Password sprayingThe same password tried against many accounts. The mirror image of a brute force. Both end in one account giving way.
Service accountAn account used by a system or a backup job rather than by a person — svc_backup here. Nobody logs into it interactively, so it usually has a long, complicated password and often no lockout policy.
LockoutWhat Windows does when one account fails too many times: it locks the account. This is the control that stops a brute force, and in this lab it was not applied to the account that was attacked.
Network logonA session created by another machine over the network, with nobody at the keyboard. Contrast a console logon, where somebody physically sat down.
Lateral movementMoving sideways: using one compromised machine to reach the next one. The attacker is not trying to get back out, they are trying to spread.
SMBWindows file sharing and remote administration, always on port 445. It is the normal way one Windows machine administers another, which is exactly why attackers use it.
PsExecA legitimate Sysinternals tool for running a command on a remote machine. It drops a small service called psexesvc.exe on the target. Administrators use it daily, so seeing it proves nothing on its own — but seeing it minutes after a brute force is another matter.

The tool

AlertA rule that fires when something looks dangerous. It is a hint, not a fact. It might be nothing at all.
ElasticsearchThe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers web addresses like localhost:9200.
KibanaThe website you do all the work in, sitting on top of Elasticsearch. Lives at localhost:5601.
IndexOne named pile of log records of the same shape. Ours are auth-* and network-*.
Data viewKibana’s word for “which pile shall I look at”. Older versions called it an index pattern.
DiscoverThe Kibana screen where you type a search and read the matching log lines. You will spend all your time here.
DocumentOne single log record. There are 561 in the auth pile and 33 in network. This is what you read.
FieldOne labelled box inside a document, like event.code. The part before the dot is the group.
KQLThe query language you type into Kibana’s search bar. field: value means “field equals value”, and and joins two conditions.
IOCIndicator of Compromise — a piece of evidence that something bad happened, e.g. an IP address, an account or a file name.
True positiveThe attack is real. Escalate it, contain it, tell someone.
False positiveNothing bad happened. Close the alert with a note saying why not.

The fields that matter most

Almost every question in this investigation is answered by four fields. Learn these and the whole lab is just typing:

  • event.code — the number of the Windows log record. It tells you what kind of thing happened. You only need three of them:
    4625 = a logon failed  ·  4624 = an account was successfully logged on  ·  4688 = a process was created
  • source.ip — the address the record came from. On a 4625 it is the machine the attempt was made from; on a 4624 it is the machine the session arrived from. Your pivot field.
  • user.name — the account being used. A brute force hammers one account, so a field that changes once is a finding.
  • host.name — the machine the record was written on, which is the machine that was attacked.
The shape of the attack, before you see it

A credential attack always has the same four beats: one address produces many failures against one account, then one of them succeeds, the account is used to reach a second machine, and a remote tool is started on it. Hold that pattern in your head. By the middle of this lab you will be hunting for it, and the number of failures will matter far less than whether the address and the account stay the same.

If the browser asks you to sign in

It will, because this lab's Kibana has security switched on. The account is lab_kibana and the password is LabKibana001. They are throwaway lab credentials that protect nothing, and you sign in once. The alert you are about to read is already waiting on the other side of that screen.

The one thing that stops most people

Docker must be installed and running. The lab runs both programs inside Docker containers. If the setup file says docker was not found, or that it is installed but not running, start it — Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux — wait until it says it is running, then run the file again. That one check fixes almost every startup problem.

What you should see

A black window that works through numbered stages. It verifies its own work as it goes, so the last thing it prints before the addresses looks like this:

The end of the setup file's own verification every document in the auth data view = 561 every document in the network data view = 33 query 1 the day's authentication events = 533 query 2 every failed logon = 104 query 3 the alerting address = 16 query 4 the one success = 1 query 5 the smb hop = 1 query 6 the remote-execution process = 1 [verify] every number the walkthrough quotes matches the live index.

Those six numbers are the answers to this whole investigation. The script has already proved them against the live index, which is why you can trust every count in the rest of this guide. Then it prints:

The last thing the setup file prints The lab is ready. Elasticsearch : http://127.0.0.1:9200 Kibana : http://127.0.0.1:5601 data view "auth" index pattern auth-* data view "network" index pattern network-*

What it did for you while you waited

So the output does not frighten you, the script performed exactly the jobs that would otherwise be the hard part of this lab:

  • Started two programs — Elasticsearch (the database) and Kibana (the website).
  • Taught Elasticsearch what each field means. An index template declares “event.code holds a number” and “source.ip holds a network address” before any data arrives. Without it Elasticsearch guesses, and guessing quietly breaks your searches.
  • Loaded the log data. If it had already loaded it, it says so and imports nothing — your data cannot load twice.
  • Created your two data views and then read them back to prove the index pattern really was stored. A data view with an empty pattern matches nothing at all, and the cause of that is invisible, so the script checks it instead of hoping.
  • Installed the detection rule and waited for it to fire. The alert you are about to read did not exist until the script did that, and the script does not print ready until the alerts are really there — 16 of them. If the rule had matched nothing, you would have been told so instead of being handed an empty page.

Completely safe. The script notices the work is done and skips it. Your data will not load twice — which matters, because duplicate documents would double every count in the rest of this guide and ruin your findings.

What you are looking at

Do this

  1. Look at the Severity levels card. Every alert is high.
  2. Find the count just above the table, next to Columns. It says 16 alerts. That is sixteen separate events, not one summary.
  3. Read the Reason column on any row. It tells you the records came from 203.0.113.45 and were for svc_backup. Write those two down.
  4. Open one alert. In the first column, called Actions, click the first small icon — the two arrows pointing outwards.

What one alert says

Two different times, and the difference matters

The alert’s own timestamp is when the rule ran — a minute or two ago, because the rule is still running every minute. The log record underneath it happened on 22 September at 10:18 UTC, in the middle of the morning. So the alerts are new and the events they point at are old, and the alerts page will keep showing them while Discover, which looks at the events themselves, shows you nothing at all until you set its time range. That is two cards away, and it is not a fault.

You are not imagining it, and nothing has gone wrong. Open one alert on the JSON tab and you will find two clocks on it:

The two timestamps, from one alert@timestamp 2026-09-30T08:06:47.567Z the day YOU ran this kibana.alert.original_time 2026-09-22T10:18:00.000Z the morning of the attack

@timestamp is when Elastic noticed. It is the day you ran the setup file, so it is a different date for every batch and it tells you nothing about the attack. kibana.alert.original_time is when the activity actually happened, and that one never moves — for this lab it is always 22 September. So: an alert is a claim that something happened; the original time is the evidence for it. Every real SOC works this way, because logs often arrive late or a rule is run against history, and if alerts were dated by the event, today’s real alerts would be buried under a wall of old ones.

Which one goes in your report? The original time. Every time you write in this lab, write the time of the activity, never the time the tool noticed it.

The rule that fired

Worth seeing, because the rule and your own investigation are the same filter.

  1. Open the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left, then Security → Rules. That is the page of detection rules; ours is the only one you have, so it sits under Custom rules. Older builds call the page Detection rules.
  2. Find the rule called Repeated failed logons from one external address, then a success on the same account.
  3. Read its query. It is (event.code: 4625 or event.code: 4624) and source.ip: "203.0.113.45" — character for character the third query in this guide.
Why this is worth two minutes

Because it means the alert count and your query count have to agree. The rule says 16, so when query 3 later returns 16 you have not merely found the same answer twice — you have found the same answer the monitoring system found, by a different road. If the two numbers ever disagree, one of them is wrong, and now you know which one to trust.

If the table is empty, it is the time picker

Not a broken lab. An alert is stamped with the time it was raised, so the range this page starts on — Today, meaning from midnight — stops covering it once you cross midnight. Click the time picker at the top right, switch to the Relative tab, and set it to 1 unit Days. The sixteen alerts come back. Some versions put a ready-made Last 24 hours button there instead, which does the same job. The lab itself never changed.

What you should have now

One rule, sixteen high alerts, risk score 73, all raised against records from 203.0.113.45 for the svc_backup account on sec-win-01. You have not run a single query yet and you already know the shape of the attack: one address, one account, one machine, and a cluster of failures with something at the end of them.

Lab is running4

Your browser just opened. Here is where you are.

no typing needed

You have read the alert. Now come to Discover, where the investigation happens — click the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left and then Discover. This card exists because this screen looks broken, and it is not — the attack was eight days ago and Discover is looking at the last few minutes, so it is simply showing you nothing yet. Here is the real screen, exactly as you are looking at it now:

Do not click “Try ES|QL” — here is what happens if you do

This build of Kibana includes ES|QL, a different query language, and the Try ES|QL button is an advert for it aimed at people who already know their way around. If you click it you will land on a screen showing this:

The error you will seeFROM logs-*-*,logs-*,filebeat-* | WHERE @timestamp >= ?_tstart AND @timestamp <= ?_tend | LIMIT 10 Unknown index [logs-*-*,logs-*,filebeat-*]

That query looks for indices called logs-* and filebeat-*. Our lab has no such indices — it has auth-* and network-*. So the query cannot work and that error is expected. It does not mean the lab is broken, and there is nothing for you to fix.

What to do instead: press the browser’s Back button to return to the screen above, then carry on. This guide only ever uses the KQL search bar.

So what is wrong right now?

Exactly one thing: the time range. The data view is fine, the search bar is fine, Kibana is healthy. The logs are simply older than the last fifteen minutes.

That is the single most common reason a beginner meets an empty screen. The Search entire time range button fixes it for you. Two cards from now you will see how to do the same thing by hand, so you can pin an exact window rather than “everything”.

Pick a pile5

Choose which pile of logs to look at

which logs?2 min

First, tell Discover which pile of logs to read. You have two of your own, and only one of them is where this attack starts.

Do this

  1. Click the dropdown on the far left of the search bar — the control with the label Data view beside it.
  2. Look at the list that opens. Kibana ships several of its own; only two entries are yours, and this is what the list looks like:
The two entries that matter, and what is in them
Data viewDocumentsHolds
auth-*561Logons, failed logons, logoffs, lockouts, privilege assignments, Kerberos pre-auth failures, program starts
network-*33Connections between machines: SMB, RPC, DNS, LDAP, HTTP, SSH, ICMP

The * is a wildcard meaning “anything starting with auth”, so a single entry covers every day of auth logs. The two piles are small, and that is the point: this is one busy day on seven servers, not a month of an estate.

You will still see no documents after closing this panel. That is correct — the time range is still the last 15 minutes. The next card fixes that.

Why this matters

A data view is a bookmark. It tells Kibana which pile of documents to read and which field holds the time. Pick the wrong one and a perfectly good query returns nothing at all, because the documents it is looking for are not in that pile.

So whenever a query returns zero results, check these three things in this order: the data view, then the time range, then the query itself. Nine times out of ten it is one of the first two, never the third.

If the sidebar says “no available fields” and stays that way

Then the data views were not created properly. Do not fight it — run the setup file again. It is safe to run twice, it reloads nothing, and it verifies each data view and tells you if anything is wrong instead of printing a hopeful message.

Be precise6

Open the time range to the right day

one click4 min

Your data is loaded and the right data view is selected. The screen is still empty for one reason only, and this card fixes it for good.

Do this

  1. Scroll back to the blue Search entire time range button in the middle of the page and click it. That is all — one click, and your records appear.
  2. Check the Documents tab. It should now read Documents (561).

Or set the exact day by hand

The button above picks the full extent of the data, which is exactly right for this lab. In a real investigation you would pin the window yourself: click the time picker (it now shows the two dates), and in the panel that opens choose the Absolute tab. Set start to Sep 22, 2026 @ 00:00:00.000 and end to Sep 22, 2026 @ 23:59:59.999, then press Update. Every query in the rest of this guide is written for that window, and it is the window you will use for the report as well.

Kibana prints numbers with a comma. Type them without one.

Watch the tables as you go. Kibana will display an event code as 4,625, and the record panel will show event.code 4,624 with a comma in it. That is display formatting, not part of the value. If you copy an event code out of the table and paste it into the search bar with the comma, you will get zero results and no error message at all. In every query, type the code plainly: 4625, 4624, 4688.

Times on your screen may not be UTC

Every timestamp in this lab is stored in UTC, and that is what the pictures in this guide show. Kibana prints times in your own computer’s timezone, which it does not let you change. If your screen is showing something else, that is not a fault and nothing is wrong with the data: write down the times from your own screen, and when you judge how far apart two events were, use the gap between them rather than the absolute clock time. The gaps are identical in every timezone, and the order never changes.

Query 17

Start wide: every authentication event of the day

baseline3 min

You now have the right data and the right day. The first move in any real triage is the same as the first move here: look at the whole picture before you go looking for anything.

Do this

  1. Click inside the search bar, clear it, and type event.category: "authentication", then press Enter.
  2. Read the number next to the Documents tab and write it down. It is not your answer, and it is deliberately big.
  3. Look at the Columns button in the toolbar and open it. In the list that appears, tick event.code, user.name, host.name and source.ip so they sit side by side, then close the panel. The Columns 6 label tells you how many are showing.
Query 1event.category: "authentication"

What the query means: event.category is the kind of record, and "authentication" is the one that means “something tried to log in”. Quotation marks around the value matter. The 28 records that are not in this result are the process-creation events — they are in the index, but they are a different category, and we will come back to them at the end.

Why this matters

This step exists to kill a very common bad instinct. A student sees “repeated failed logons” in an alert, runs one broad query, gets a lot of rows, and either panics or shrugs. A large number is not a finding. What you are hunting is a shape: one address, one account, and a very specific imbalance between failures and successes. You cannot see that until you stop looking at everything.

Prove it8

Prove that 533 really is a dead end

negative result3 min

Before you narrow anything, let us be certain that 533 is nothing to work with. Kibana can count the distinct values in a field for you, which turns “there is a lot of it” into a sentence you can put in a report.

Do this

  1. Click the Field statistics tab, next to Documents. Nothing else changes: the query and the time range stay exactly as they were.
  2. Read the Distinct values column, top to bottom, and write the four numbers next to their field names.
  3. Click Documents again when you have finished. You are back on the rows.
What the dead end is worth

A negative result is a result. You have now established, with numbers, that “authentication activity” and “failed logons” on their own are not anomalies on this estate — there are six kinds of event, nine accounts and eleven addresses, all flat across the day. If you had stopped here you would have written “nothing unusual” and closed a real attack.

Say exactly this in your report. “I checked the whole population first and it is flat” is what separates a real investigation from a lucky guess.

Query 29

Every failed logon of the day — and the trap in it

the wrong answer is in here4 min

Now narrow to the thing the alert actually mentions: failures. Do this one properly, because the answer to it is wrong on purpose.

Do this

  1. Replace the query in the search bar with event.code: 4625 and press Enter.
  2. Read the Documents count and write it down.
  3. Sort by the user.name column if the count is not what you expected, and look for the busiest account. That account is the wrong one. Keep reading.
  4. Sort back to @timestamp so the day reads left to right.
Query 2event.code: 4625

What the query means: 4625 is the Windows record written every time an account fails to log on. One row is one failed attempt, so 104 rows is 104 wrong passwords.

The trap, and why it is there

Every account here is a person typing a password wrongly through a week, and they fail a handful of times each. The four other addresses (192.0.2.10, 192.0.2.24, 198.51.100.7, 198.51.100.42) each produce more failures across the whole day than the alerting address does in its sixteen minutes, scattered across ten hours.

So the account with the most failures is not the account that was attacked. If you report “an account was attacked 104 times today” you have reported nothing, and if you pick the top row of a sorted table you have picked the wrong account. The number of failures is not the finding. The address and the account are the finding.

The control that should have stopped this — and did not

While you are here, check one thing that decides how bad this is. Windows has a lockout control: after too many failures an account is locked, and the alert here is 4740. There are 41 lockouts in this data, all of them for other accounts, all of them local.

Now search user.name: "svc_backup" and read the result. Then try user.name: "svc_backup" and event.code: 4740. Nothing. The account under attack had no lockout policy at all, which is normal for service accounts and is the reason this attack had time to run. That is a finding of its own, and it belongs in your recommendations.

Query 310

The alerting address. This is the finding.

the primary evidence5 min

Now do what a real analyst does: take the one value the alert gave you — the address 203.0.113.45 — and put it next to the failures. This is the same query the shorter companion brief (instructions.md) gives you as its single one-shot question.

Do this

  1. Replace the query in the search bar with the one in the box below and press Enter.
  2. Read the Documents count and write it down. It should match the number of alerts on the page you started from.
  3. Read down the event.code and event.outcome columns. Most rows are one thing and a small number of rows are the other. Write down both numbers.
  4. Look at the first and last @timestamp in the list and work out how long the run took. Write down the span.
Query 3 — the alerting address(event.code: 4625 or event.code: 4624) and source.ip: "203.0.113.45"

What the query means, clause by clause: event.code: 4625 or event.code: 4624 — keep both outcomes, failures and successes, because you do not yet know which one matters. source.ip: "203.0.113.45" — only the address from the alert, quotes included. and — both must be true. The result is every authentication event that address ever produced, which is precisely the set the rule matched.

The shape, and what a false positive would look like instead

You have 15 failures and 1 success, all from one address, all against one account, all on one host, inside 16 minutes. The last row is not a failure — read its event.code before you write the report, because the difference between “many failures” and “a break-in” is one field in one row.

A suspicious picture is this: one address, one account, a tight run of failures, and then a success inside the same window. A benign picture looks different in every one of those four respects: a handful of failures spread over hours from addresses that also produce successes all day, and never a success that follows a burst from the same address.

Query 411

Isolate the one that worked

who got in4 min

Sixteen rows, fifteen failures, and one that is not. Now take the failures out and look at what is left, field by field.

Do this

  1. Replace the query in the search bar with the one below and press Enter.
  2. Confirm the Documents count says 1.
  3. Click the small ⇉ two-arrows icon at the left of the row to open the whole record, and read every field, not just the columns you have on screen.
  4. Write down the account, the host name, the host address and the timestamp. This is the centre of your report.
Query 4 — the success onlyevent.code: 4624 and source.ip: "203.0.113.45"

What the query means: 4624 is the record written when an account is successfully logged on. Adding it to the previous query is what separates a brute force that broke in from a brute force that failed. Do not skip the parenthesis in the previous query when you copy this pattern for your own report.

Three things to say out loud about that row
  1. It is a service account. svc_backup belongs to a backup job, not to a person. Nobody sits at a keyboard to run a backup, so a human logon for it from a server on the internet is not a thing that happens.
  2. The account appears nowhere else all day. Search user.name: "svc_backup" on its own: you get 16 documents, and every one of them is from this address during this run. A service account that has been quietly working for months has a history — and this one has none.
  3. It was not locked out. 41 other accounts were locked during the day; this one had no policy, so the 15 attempts were free.
Query 512

What the broken-into machine did next

new data view4 min

You have the account and the first machine: svc_backup on sec-win-01, address 10.0.4.10. The authentication logs can only tell you about logins. To see what happened next, switch to the other pile — the traffic logs.

Do this

  1. Click the Data view dropdown again and choose network-* this time. The time range and the columns stay as they are — they belong to the screen, not to the pile.
  2. Type the query in the box below and press Enter.
  3. Read the Documents count, then read across the row: source, destination, port, bytes, timestamp. Write them all down.
  4. Take the destination.ip from the row and search the auth-* pile for it. That is how you learn the name of the machine you have just found.
Query 5 — on the network-* data viewnetwork.protocol: "smb" and source.ip: "10.0.4.10"

What the query means, clause by clause: network.protocol: "smb" — only SMB traffic, and SMB is always port 445. source.ip: "10.0.4.10" — only connections leaving the machine that was just broken into. and — both. Both halves come from what you just found: nothing in this query was given to you, and that is what makes it evidence rather than a guess.

This is lateral movement, and here is the proof that it is

Three things have to line up, and you have all three:

  • the connection starts on the machine that was just broken into — not from the attacker’s address, which is a physical path you cannot see, but from the victim itself;
  • it goes to a different internal machine, 10.0.4.12, which no other query in this lab has mentioned;
  • it is four minutes after the successful logon, and it uses the protocol Windows administrators use every day to run commands on another server.

Do not skip the timestamp. An SMB connection between two servers is the most ordinary event in a Windows network; an SMB connection four minutes after a brute force is the same bytes with a completely different meaning.

Query 613

What the second machine was made to run

the end of the chain4 min

One hop, one protocol, one destination. Now find out what arrived. You do not know the process name yet, so start from the one piece of the story you are certain of: the second machine, 10.0.4.12.

Do this

  1. First, name that machine. Switch back to auth-* and run host.ip: "10.0.4.12". One document, and it tells you the host.name — sec-win-02. Write it down: you now know a name for the address the traffic query gave you, and a name belongs in a report.
  2. Notice how little that machine does all day. It has one record in the whole authentication pile. Nobody logs in to it. Nothing logs off from it.
  3. Now ask the process question. Look in the event.code column while you do it: process creation is 4688, and its category is process, which is why it was not in query 1.
  4. Run the query in the box below, open the row, and read every field — especially the parent process and the account it ran as.
Query 6 — on the auth-* data viewprocess.name: "psexesvc.exe"

What the query means: process.name is the name of the program that started. This one is the service half of PsExec, the Sysinternals tool administrators use to run a command on a remote machine. A search on a process name is the only kind of query in this lab that does not need an address or an account — because at this point you are asking “what landed on the target?”, and the answer is one file name.

Put it together14

Four findings, one chain

this is the case

You have everything. Before you write a word, look at the four findings as a single sequence, because the sequence is the argument — a pile of facts proves nothing.

What each query added

QueryResultWhat it proves
event.category: "authentication"533The whole authentication population of the day — and that it is flat, boring and useless on its own
event.code: 4625104Failures are normal here, they come from five addresses, and the busiest account is not the attacked one
(event.code: 4625 or event.code: 4624) and source.ip: "203.0.113.45"16One address, one account, one host, fifteen failures in a row and then a success
event.code: 4624 and source.ip: "203.0.113.45"1The break-in itself: svc_backup on sec-win-01 at 10:18:00.000, and an account with no history and no lockout
network.protocol: "smb" and source.ip: "10.0.4.10"1Lateral movement: the compromised machine reached 10.0.4.12 on port 445, four minutes later
process.name: "psexesvc.exe"1Remote execution: PsExec started by services.exe as SYSTEM on sec-win-02, three minutes later

The chain, in one line each

  1. Brute force. 203.0.113.45 fails to log on as svc_backup 15 times against sec-win-01 between 10:00:00 and 10:16:00, roughly one a minute.
  2. Break-in. At 10:18:00.000 the same address, the same account, this time accepted. It is a service account, it has no other activity all day, and it had no lockout policy.
  3. Lateral movement. At 10:22:00.000 the new session opens one SMB connection from 10.0.4.10 to 10.0.4.12:445 — a second machine.
  4. Execution. At 10:25:00.000 psexesvc.exe starts on that second machine, parent services.exe, account SYSTEM.
Twenty-five minutes, start to finish

Read the four times against each other. The first failure and the last piece of remote execution are 25 minutes apart, and every step is later than the one before it. There is no step out of order, and no step hours away from its neighbour.

That tightness is itself evidence. It rules out coincidence, it rules out a scheduled job, and it rules out an administrator having a busy morning. One person or one script did all four things, in this order, in twenty-five minutes.

Now ask the questions that turn facts into a verdict

QuestionYour answer, and the query that proved it
Who started it?source.ip: 203.0.113.45, on 16 of 16 records
What did they want?svc_backup - a service account with no history and no lockout
How did they get in?15 failed logons in 16 minutes, then 1 success — a brute force that worked
How far did they get?two machines: sec-win-01 (10.0.4.10), then sec-win-02 (10.0.4.12)
Why is it not routine?the account never appears outside this window, and the second machine has one record all day: the process
The one-sentence verdict

On 22 September 2026 an external address, 203.0.113.45, made fifteen failed logon attempts against the service account svc_backup on sec-win-01 in sixteen minutes, succeeded on the sixteenth at 10:18:00 UTC, and four minutes later used that session to open one SMB connection to a second server, sec-win-02 (10.0.4.12), where psexesvc.exe was started as SYSTEM three minutes after that.

That is a true positive. Every clause of that sentence is traceable to one of the six queries you just ran. That is what a finished investigation looks like.

Put it together15

Build the timeline

most important 5 min

This is the most important 5 minutes in the lab. Investigators do not just collect facts — they arrange them so the facts argue the conclusion for them.

Do this

Open a text file (Notepad is fine) and write five lines, oldest first, copying the times off your own screen. The yellow blank is your work — read it off your table and type it in. The gaps on the right are pre-filled, because gaps are the same in every timezone and they are the actual evidence.

  1. 10:00:00.000  →  fill in from your screen
    The brute force. 15 failed logons (4625, event.outcome failure) for svc_backup on sec-win-01 from 203.0.113.45, one a minute, two minutes missing. 16 minutes and 0.9 seconds in total.
  2. 10:18:00.000  (+1 min 59 s)
    The break-in. One successful logon (4624, success) for the same account, from the same address, on the same host. A service account, no lockout, and nowhere else in the day’s 561 records.
  3. 10:22:00.000  (+4 min)
    Lateral movement. SMB connection 10.0.4.10:49,156 → 10.0.4.12:445, 5,164 bytes, written on sec-win-01. The first thing the new session did was reach sec-win-02.
  4. 10:25:00.000  (+3 min)
    Remote execution. psexesvc.exe created on sec-win-02 (4688, category process), creator services.exe, running as SYSTEM from C:\Windows\system32.
  5. 10:25:00.000  →  17:59:36.873  (the rest of the day)
    Nothing. No further logons for svc_backup, no more traffic from 203.0.113.45, no other process on sec-win-02. The attacker used the access once and was gone — which is what staging looks like, and why the follow-up hunt matters more than the response.

The clock times above are UTC, which is how the lab stores them and how this guide’s pictures were taken. If your screen is showing a different offset, write down your numbers instead — what matters is that the five lines stay in this order and keep these gaps: 16 minutes of failures, then 2, 4, 3 minutes from there to the end.

The shape of the answer

A normal, noisy, ten-hour day of logins — and then, in twenty-five minutes starting at 10:00, everything in this lab happens, in strict order: failures, success, hop, execution. Nothing is hours apart, nothing is days apart, and nothing comes before the thing that would have to come first.

That tightness is itself evidence. It rules out coincidence, and it rules out routine administration.

Deliverable16

Write the report, then prove it

25 mindo not skip

Nobody reads your screen. This card is the deliverable — it is the thing you hand in, and it is the only place in the guide you type. It has two parts and both go into your submission: Part one is your written report, Part two is the set of figures you checked off your own screen as you went. Neither part has an answer printed next to it. Fill both in, then press EXPORT MY SUBMISSION at the bottom: a finished PDF report lands in your Downloads folder with your name and batch number on the front of it.

Do this yourself, and do it now

If you cannot fill a line in without going back to Kibana, you have not finished the investigation — which is exactly the point. These fields are deliberately empty and stay that way until you type. Nothing here is marked against a model answer; it is marked on whether you found these things.

Both of these are printed at the top of the exported PDF and go into the file name, so the submission is identifiable without you having to say who you are in the report itself. Leave either one blank and the file still exports — it just says [not answered] where your name should be, which is a good reason not to leave them blank.

Part one — your report

1. Summary

What happened

two or three sentences a manager could follow, and no jargon in the first sentence

2. Timeline

When

one line per stage, oldest first, with the times read off your own screen — not off this guide

3. Evidence

How you know

each query you ran, the number it returned, and what that number proved. The number matters as much as the reasoning — especially the numbers you ruled out

4. Impact

What is affected

the account, every machine involved, and how much you can say about what the attacker did with the access

5. Verdict

True positive or false positive

state it plainly in the first line, then the whole chain in one paragraph

6. Recommendations

What should happen next

concrete actions in the order you would carry them out: contain, then eradicate, then harden. Include the control that failed, which is the lockout policy on a service account

Every line below is a number you should be able to point at on your own screen. These travel with your report, so a figure that contradicts your writing gives you away — if Part one and Part two disagree, one of them is wrong, and you want to know which before you hand it in.

Your verdict in one line

Two things worth double-checking in your own report

These are the two that catch people out, so read yours back now:

  1. Did you say which address and which account? A report that stops at “event.code: 4625 returned 104 results and the failures look normal” is incomplete, and worse, a report that names the account with the most failures is wrong — that is the busiest innocent account, not the one that was attacked. The event code on its own is not a finding.
  2. Did you separate the two days in the timeline? The attack is 25 minutes long inside a ten-hour day. If your report gives the impression that the whole day was attack, you have over-claimed, and a reader who checks will stop believing the rest of it.

And one bonus: if you looked at host.ip: "10.0.4.12" and noticed that the second machine has one single record in the whole day — the process you just found — say so. It is not required, and nothing checks it automatically, but it is the sentence that turns a list of counts into a story.

The PDF lands in your Downloads folder; nothing is uploaded and no internet connection is needed.

Finish17

Tear the lab down

one file1 min

One file removes everything the lab created. Nothing is left running, and nothing of yours is deleted.

Do this

  1. Make sure you have submitted your report. The teardown deletes the data.
  2. Close your browser and every Kibana tab.
  3. In the lab folder, run the teardown file for your system: on Windows, double-click teardown.cmd; on macOS or Linux, run ./teardown.sh in a terminal in that folder (or bash teardown.sh).
  4. It prints the exact list of what it is about to remove, and asks you to confirm (Y or N on Windows, y or n on macOS and Linux). Read the list, then say yes.
  5. It finishes by verifying the removal and telling you what was kept.
The list the teardown file prints before it deletes anything The following will be REMOVED. Nothing else will be touched. container brute-force-001-elasticsearch container brute-force-001-kibana volume brute-force-001_esdata (this holds ALL the lab data) file .../brute-force-001/docker-compose.yml folder .../elklab-brute-force-001

Yours will show a different path — a Windows path on Windows, a /var/folders/... or /tmp/ one on a Mac. The five names are the same everywhere, and only the names are ever deleted.

What it will never touch

Every name in that list is derived from the folder name, and nothing else is considered for deletion. In particular:

  • No Docker images are removed. They are large and slow to download, so they are kept and the next setup is fast and works offline.
  • No other container or volume on this machine is touched, so a second lab running beside this one is safe.
  • Your files stay. The log data, the templates and this guide are all still in the folder afterwards.

The teardown file never runs docker system prune and never removes an image. It says so on screen before it starts, and it means it.

If you would rather just stop it and keep the data

Sometimes you want the lab back tomorrow without waiting for it to reload. Stop the containers but keep everything, and start them again later with one command:

Run this in a terminal, in the lab folderdocker compose -f docker-compose.yml down

Your data lives in the Docker volume, so it survives. Bring it all back with docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d, or simply run the setup file again — it is safe to run twice and will not re-import anything.

Running teardown twice is harmless

It checks what is actually there first, tells you there is nothing to do, and exits. It will not complain and it will not delete anything else looking for something to clean up. That matters, because people run it twice to be sure.

Reference18

If something goes wrong

not a steplook me up

Four things account for almost every problem in this lab. Work down the list rather than guessing.

1. The screen is empty and there are no documents

Almost never a broken query. Check, in this order:

  1. Is the data view right? It must say auth-* for queries 1 to 4 and 6, and network-* for query 5.
  2. Is the time range right? If it says Last 15 minutes, the data is older than that and you will see nothing. Click Search entire time range again. This is by far the most common cause, and it happens after pressing F5 or navigating away and back.
  3. Is the query in the bar at all? It should be in plain text, not in a leftover filter row underneath.
If the Alerts page is the empty one

Same cause, different page. An alert is stamped with the time the rule ran, not the time the event happened, so the alerts page starts on Today and the log data is from September 2026. If the Alerts page is empty, set its time picker to Last 24 hours or 1 day and the sixteen come back. The alert card explains the two timestamps, because this one catches everyone out at least once.

2. A query returns 0 documents when you expect 16, 104 or 533

You seeWhat it almost certainly means
0, and you typed event.code: 4,625The comma. Kibana displays numbers with a comma; you must type 4625. Same for 4624 and 4688, and same for ports and byte counts.
0, and you dropped the quotation markssource.ip: 203.0.113.45 and process.name: psexesvc.exe both need the quotes, because both values contain dots. Copy the query from the dark box instead of typing it.
0, and you dropped the brackets(event.code: 4625 or event.code: 4624) and source.ip: "203.0.113.45" needs them. Without them, and binds to the second clause only and you lose every failure.
0, and you are on the network-* viewQueries 1–4 and 6 are on auth-*. Only query 5 belongs to network-*.

3. The counts do not match this guide

You seeWhat it almost certainly means
Double every numberThe data was imported twice. Run the setup file with reset and then it again, which rebuilds the data exactly once.
217 instead of 217Nothing wrong — that is event.code: 4625 or event.code: 4624, which nobody asks for in this guide. If you want it, that is 104 failures plus 113 successes.
1 instead of 16 for query 3You pasted query 4 by mistake, or you dropped the 4625 half of the or.
Times are hours offThat is your timezone, not a fault. Read the gaps, not the absolute clock times — see the time-range card.
Dates in the past, on a computer years aheadExpected, and not a fault. The log data is a real day in September 2026 and never moves. The rule that raises the alerts only looks back a year, so it keeps finding it.
The sidebar says 0 available fieldsStill a time-range problem. Click Search entire time range.
Event codes shown as 4,625 and 4,624Display formatting, and the number of the record is 4625 and 4624. The Table tab in the Document panel shows the same comma.

4. The lab will not start

What the setup file saysWhat to do
docker was not foundDocker is not installed. Ask your instructor.
Docker is installed but the engine is not respondingOpen Docker Desktop and wait until it says it is running, then run the file again.
something else is already using port 9200Another lab is running. The script refuses to touch it, correctly. Stop the other one, or run teardown.cmd from the folder that owns it.
a container called brute-force-001-elasticsearch already existsThe folder was copied or moved, so a previous copy owns the container. The script shows you the details and stops without deleting anything. Follow the two docker commands it prints, or run teardown.cmd from the original folder first.
Elasticsearch did not become ready in timeIt prints the last 40 lines of the container log. Usually not enough memory for Docker; close other applications, or give Docker Desktop more memory in its settings.
the auth index holds N documents but this lab ships 561A partial load. The script refuses to import on top of it, because that would create duplicates. Run setup-lab.cmd reset.
rule.json is missingPut rule.json back in the folder and run the setup file again. Everything else is already loaded; only the Alerts page needs it.

Two controls that catch people out

  • Clicking a table row does nothing. You need the small ⇉ two-diagonal-arrows button immediately to the left of the @timestamp column. In the Document panel, Escape closes it.
  • The Field statistics tab shows one row per FIELD, not one row per value. It will not give you “113 and 104” style counts — for an exact number, run the query and read the Documents tab.
The 30-second checklist

Data view right? → Time range says a date, not “Last 15 minutes”? → Query text in the bar, with the brackets and the quotes and no commas? → Number in the Documents tab matches the number this guide quotes? If all four are true and something still looks wrong, press F5 and re-click Search entire time range, then re-run the queries from the top. If Query 1 does not return a large number of documents, your time range is still wrong; if it does, the problem is in the query text rather than in the dates.

The coloured markings

Yellow means a value you must read off your own screen and write down — that is your work. There is deliberately no second colour: nothing in this guide is filled in for you, and no answer key is printed anywhere inside it.

Stuck on a step?

Almost every problem in this lab has one of three causes, and all three are on the If it breaks card near the end: the time range reset, the wrong data view, or Docker not running. Go there rather than guessing.
